title: Official talk
job: Announcements, offices and counters: the formal register you hear
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: THE PASSIVE ENTERS HERE, AND TWO MODULES PROMISED IT. L2-M8's frāctus est and L3-M6's sollicitus sum were taught as ADJECTIVES with sum, both said out loud that the construction was a passive in full Latin, and both pointed at this module. The real thing is an ending: -tur in the singular, -ntur in the plural. clauditur 'it is closed', vetātur 'it is forbidden', dantur 'they are issued'. Against the active -t and -nt, the difference is three letters carrying the entire question of who is doing it.

THE PASSIVE IS OPENED IN THE THIRD PERSON ONLY, AND THAT IS ENOUGH FOR AN ANNOUNCEMENT. A passive of every person in every tense is a system twice the size of this module; an announcement needs exactly 'it is closed' and 'they are issued' — nobody named as closing or issuing, which is what the passive is FOR. L2-M8's participle-as-adjective arrangement stands for everything else, and S06 puts both in one sentence so the difference is visible: dīcitur has the ending, clausam agrees.

AN ANNOUNCEMENT NAMES NOBODY, AND THAT IS A REGISTER RATHER THAN AN EVASION. Things close, forms are issued, entering is forbidden — the institution never appears as a subject, which is the same shape English uses on a sign. Every sentence in this module carries the formal chip (#422), and en-la's formal is STILL NOT A PRONOUN: L2-M1 settled that politeness rides on the verb and that vōs to one person is simply wrong, and official Latin adds the impersonal passive to that rather than a pronoun. vōs appears nowhere in this module.

A SIGN DROPS EVERYTHING A READER CAN SUPPLY, INCLUDING est. M1 taught legendum est and said est was not optional; nōn intrandum on a wall has no est at all, because inscriptional Latin leaves out what a reader will fill in. That is a register, not an exception — and it is the register this module exists for.

cavē TAKES A PLAIN OBJECT AND ENGLISH NEEDS 'OF'. cavē canem is 'beware the dog', and it is the sixth construction in this course where an English preposition has nowhere to attach — after raedā, hōrā, auxilium rogō, mūsicam audiō and eum exspectō. It is also the most famous two words of Latin ever laid in a floor.

AN ABBREVIATION IS WRITTEN WITHOUT DOTS IN THIS COURSE, AND THE REASON IS THE INDEX. Run against the real src/engine/surface.ts: SPQR normalizes to spqr and S.P.Q.R. normalizes to s.p.q.r, because rule 3 strips a TRAILING dot and keeps the interior ones. So the dotted and undotted spellings are two different keys for one thing, and a learner tapping one would be shown nothing about the other. This course writes SPQR and names D.M. and every other dotted abbreviation in prose only. SPQR stands for Senātus Populusque Rōmānus, and the -que inside it is L1-M10's enclitic doing its ordinary job.

A PASSIVE CAN REPORT, AND dīcitur IS HOW. L3-M5 taught dīcit sē venīre with a named speaker; dīcitur officīnam clausam esse says it with nobody at all — 'it is said that'. The reported clause is unchanged, accusative and infinitive as always, and what has gone is the person doing the saying. That is the most useful single shape in official Latin, because it lets you relay something without vouching for it.

sentences.cue: The office closes at the ninth hour.

words.note: 'Office, workshop' — a classical word put to a modern use by the living-Latin community. L3-M8's row, and officīnae is more than one.
'At the hour' — L3-M1's ablative, and the ending is the 'at'.
'Ninth', agreeing with hōrā. L3-M1's word, and the ninth hour is mid-afternoon.
'It is closed' — a PASSIVE, and the -tur ending is what makes it one. claudō is 'I close'; clauditur is 'it is closed', with nobody named as closing it.

sentences.trap: THE PASSIVE ARRIVES, and L2-M8 and L3-M6 both promised it here. Those modules taught frāctus est and sollicitus sum as ADJECTIVES with sum and said out loud that the construction was a passive in full Latin. This is the real thing: a -tur ending, and nobody named as doing it.
sentences.sound: of-fi-CĪ-na HŌ-rā NŌ-nā CLAU-di-tur. Ten syllables and three long vowels before the verb.

mistake.why: the active ending on a passive sentence. claudit would mean the office closes something else — and the whole point of an announcement is that nobody is named as doing the closing, which is the job only a passive can do.

'It is forbidden' — passive, from vetō 'I forbid'. An announcement forbids without saying who is forbidding, which is what the passive is for.

sentences.trap: Nobody forbids and nobody enters. Official Latin says what is not done without saying who says so or who would do it — which is exactly the register the job means, and the impersonal passive is the one shape that manages both at once.

sentences.cue: It is said that the office is closed.

words.note: 'It is said' — passive, from dīcō. L3-M5 taught dīcit for a named speaker; this says it with nobody at all.
'Office' in the OBJECT shape, because the clause is reported. L3-M8's word inside L3-M3's construction.
'Closed' — a participle used as an ADJECTIVE, agreeing with officīnam. L2-M8's frāctus arrangement, which this module's passive does not replace.
'To be' — sum's infinitive. L3-M3's word.

sentences.trap: A passive verb reporting an adjective that looks passive. dīcitur is the real passive and clausam esse is L2-M8's participle-as-adjective — so one sentence has both arrangements in it, and the difference is that dīcitur has a -tur ending and clausam agrees.

words.note: 'Here'. L1-M7's word.
'Forms, papers' — charta for one, chartae for more than one. L3-M8's word, and the plural is fresh.
'They are given' — the passive of L1-M8's dā, plural. dat is 'he gives', datur 'it is given', dantur 'they are given': -ntur is the plural passive.

sentences.trap: dat and dantur are the same verb and opposite voices. L3-M9 taught dat, dant and damus in the active; this is the passive, and the whole difference is -ntur against -nt — one letter in the middle, carrying the entire question of who is doing it.

sentences.cue: The office is closing; forms are issued tomorrow.

words.note: 'Office' as the subject.
'It is closed' — a PASSIVE, and the -tur ending is what makes it one. claudō is 'I close'; clauditur is 'it is closed', with nobody named as closing it.
'Tomorrow'. L1-M4's word, and one of six caseless time adverbs.
'Forms' — charta for one, chartae for more than one.
'They are given' — the passive of dā, plural.

sentences.trap: Two passives in two clauses and nobody named in either. That is what official Latin sounds like: things close, forms are issued, and the institution never appears as a subject — which is a register rather than an evasion, and it is the same one English uses on a sign.
